turns.name: P1-intro
turns.question: Pick the one project that best shows your mobile skills. Who used it, what problem did it solve, and where did your responsibility start and end?

card.problem: Walk through a project the candidate really owned (KKday AI trip planner)
card.heard: pick the project that best shows my mobile skills
card.say: The AI trip planner at KKday is the one I'd pick. Travelers used it in our Android app to plan a real trip. They typed something like "Tokyo, 5,000 yuan, three days", and the app gave them a day-by-day plan they could book. I was the technical lead for a five-person project. My responsibility started with the agent design and the core backend.
card.then: Wait for the interviewer to pick a part to go deeper on.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer names a real Android project (KKday AI trip planner), its users (travelers), the problem (planning a trip to a budget/duration), and the candidate's scope (technical lead, agent design and core backend), with no invented employers, titles, or numbers.
judge.criterion: SAY introduces one real Android project from the candidate's background with its users, the problem and the candidate's own scope; no invented employers, titles or numbers.

turns.name: P1-dyn
turns.question: On the KKday AI trip planner, you said your responsibility started with agent design and the core backend — so which exact pieces did you build yourself, and which parts did the five-person team own?

card.problem: Walk through a project the candidate really owned (KKday AI trip planner)
card.heard: which exact pieces I built, which the team owned
card.say: I built the agent design and the core backend myself. I also wrote the Android code that reads the SSE stream of the plan. The other four people owned the app screens, the product side and the testing. I set the response format with the app team, but they built the cards.
card.then: Wait for the interviewer to pick a part to go deeper on.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer specifies concrete pieces (agent design, core backend, SSE-reading Android code), distinguishes team ownership (screens, product, testing, cards), stays consistent with the earlier technical-lead claim, and invents no employer, title, metric, or wallet rule.
judge.criterion: The answer follows from what the candidate said, adds something specific rather than repeating the previous answer, stays consistent with the candidate's earlier answers and background, is technically correct, and invents no employer, title, metric or wallet rule the interviewer did not give.

turns.name: P2-change
turns.question: Pick a change you personally made. Walk me from one user action through the UI, data or network path. Which logic did you actually change?

card.problem: Walk through a project the candidate really owned (KKday AI trip planner)
card.heard: pick a change I personally made, walk one user action through the path
card.say: The change I made myself is the SKU calculation on the product page. A user taps a date, a package or a ticket type. Before, every tap recalculated all the price and stock combinations on the main thread. I flattened the configuration and built a price and stock index once. Then I moved the work to Dispatchers.Default and sent results back through StateFlow.
card.then: Next I can go deeper on the index or on the StateFlow part.

more: The index is rebuilt only when the configuration version changes, so a stale index can't serve prices after a catalog update.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer traces a tap through UI, main-thread recalculation, a flattened price/stock index, Dispatchers.Default, and StateFlow; it names the changed logic (SKU calculation) as the candidate's own, and gives no invented numbers.
judge.criterion: SAY traces one user action through concrete layers (UI, state, data or network) and says which logic the candidate changed; separates own work from the team's; no invented numbers.

turns.name: P2-bug
turns.question: What was the hardest bug to reproduce there? What did you suspect first, and which log, experiment or repro proved you wrong?

card.problem: Walk through a project the candidate really owned (KKday AI trip planner)
card.heard: hardest bug to reproduce, what I suspected, what proved me wrong
card.say: The hardest one was a wrong price after a catalog update. I suspected the calculation first, but the numbers were correct. The real cause was the cached index. It was still the old version, so the page showed old prices. I reproduced it by changing the configuration while the page was open.
card.then: Wait for the interviewer.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer gives a clear timeline — initial suspicion (the calculation), evidence overturning it (numbers were correct), and root cause (stale cached index), plus a repro (changing config while page open); it distinguishes observation from conclusion and says nothing wrong.
judge.criterion: SAY gives a timeline: first suspicion, the evidence (log, experiment or repro) that overturned it, and the root cause, distinguishing observation from conclusion.

turns.name: P2-dyn
turns.question: You said you reproduced it by changing the configuration while the page was open — how did you confirm the stale index was actually the cause and not just a coincidence?

card.problem: Walk through a project the candidate really owned (KKday AI trip planner)
card.heard: how did you confirm the stale index was the cause
card.say: I checked the version number in the log against the one the page was using. They didn't match, so the page was reading an old index. Then I forced a rebuild and the price was correct. That proved it wasn't a coincidence.
card.then: Wait for the interviewer.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer builds directly on the candidate's earlier stale-index repro, adds a specific confirmation method (comparing the logged version number to the page's version, then forcing a rebuild to see the correct price), stays consistent with the prior account, and invents no new employer, title, metric, or wallet rule.
judge.criterion: The answer follows from what the candidate said, adds something specific rather than repeating the previous answer, stays consistent with the candidate's earlier answers and background, is technically correct, and invents no employer, title, metric or wallet rule the interviewer did not give.

turns.name: P2-alt
turns.question: What other options did you have, why didn't you pick them, and after release how did you know the change worked?

card.problem: Walk through a project the candidate really owned (KKday AI trip planner)
card.heard: other options, why not, how did you know it worked after release
card.say: There were two other options. First, I could rebuild the index on every tap, but that's the slow path we were fixing. Second, I could keep the old index and just refresh it on a timer, but a timer still serves stale prices for a while. I picked the version check because it's exact and cheap. After release, I watched crash and ANR reports, and I checked that the version in the log matched the page.
card.then: Wait for the interviewer.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer names two alternatives (rebuild on every tap, timer-based refresh) with the constraint ruling each out (slow path, stale prices), and gives post-release evidence (crash/ANR reports, log version match) — though it could note limits of that evidence, it says nothing wrong and covers the required points.
judge.criterion: SAY names a real alternative and the constraint that ruled it out, and the source of the result (metric, test, ticket or feedback) with its limits.

turns.name: P3-risk
turns.question: Tell me about a time you saw a delivery risk or a likely delay and the team disagreed. When did you tell whom, how many options did you give, who decided, and what did you finish yourself?

card.problem: Tell me about a delivery risk where the team disagreed: when I told whom, the options, who decided, what I finished myself
card.heard: delivery risk, team disagreed, who decided
card.say: At Debon, I found a broken back button just before a release. Some pages jumped to the home screen instead of the stock details. I told the project manager the same day, before I had checked every page. I gave two options: ship everything and accept the risk, or keep the old pages and move my change to the next release. He decided to move my change.
card.then: Wait for the interviewer.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer gives a concrete Debon case, states he told the project manager the same day, offers two options, names the PM as decider, and describes his own change being moved to the next release.
judge.criterion: SAY describes one concrete case: when and whom the candidate told, the options offered, who had the decision, and what the candidate personally did; attributes the case to the right company.

turns.name: P3-dyn
turns.question: On the Debon release where you moved your change, what risk were you willing to accept by shipping, who watched the data afterwards, and what signal would have made you pause or roll back?

card.problem: Tell me about a delivery risk where the team disagreed: when I told whom, the options, who decided, what I finished myself
card.heard: what risk did you accept by shipping, who watched the data, what signal would pause or roll back
card.say: We shipped everything else, so the risk I accepted was the old pages staying as they were. The back button still jumped to the home screen on those two pages, but nothing else changed. I told the project manager that risk clearly before he decided. After release, I watched the crash reports in Bugly myself, and I asked QA to check the back button on the old pages. If the crash rate had gone up, or if users had reported the back button more often, I would have paused the release and rolled back.
card.then: Wait for the interviewer.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer stays consistent with the earlier Debon story (moving his change, old pages kept), adds specifics like Bugly crash reports and QA checks, names a concrete rollback signal, and invents no new employer, title, or metric.
judge.criterion: The answer follows from what the candidate said, adds something specific rather than repeating the previous answer, stays consistent with the candidate's earlier answers and background, is technically correct, and invents no employer, title, metric or wallet rule the interviewer did not give.

turns.name: W1-scope
turns.question: Let's switch to the design exercise. Design a mobile wallet from scratch: the core mobile experience, the system behind it, and how it handles failures. Start by clarifying the requirements. Which user path would you define as the MVP?

card.problem: Design a mobile wallet: core mobile experience, backend, failure handling; clarify requirements and define the MVP path
card.heard: switch to design exercise — clarify requirements, define MVP path
card.say: Before I design anything, let me confirm the scope. The MVP is one person sending money to another person they know, by phone number or contact, with a clear result on screen. Out of scope for now: paying merchants, cards, and multiple currencies. On the non-functional side, the money must never be lost or sent twice, and the user must always know whether it went through. Does that match what you want?
card.then: Once you confirm, I'll draw the main flow: the send screen, the server, and the result screen.

more: A timeout is not a failure; it's an unknown outcome, so the app asks the server again with the same transfer ID.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer proposes a clear MVP path (person-to-person send by phone/contact) and clarifies scope (out of scope: merchants, cards, multiple currencies; non-functional: no lost/duplicate money, clear outcome), covering at least two of the listed examples without saying anything wrong.
judge.criterion: SAY asks clarifying questions about scope (stored balance vs external rail, currency, offline behaviour, authority of the ledger) and proposes one MVP path such as send money to a contact.

turns.name: W2-design
turns.question: Here are the rules: signed-in users, centralized balance accounts, single currency USD, internal peer-to-peer transfers, zero fees. Balance, transfer, history and details are in scope. Cached reads work offline; submitting money needs the network. The server owns the authoritative ledger and limits. Top-up, withdrawal and multi-currency are out of scope. A has 100 dollars and B has zero. Draw the client, the server and local storage as a flowchart, and tell me what each part owns.

card.problem: Design a mobile wallet: core mobile experience, backend, failure handling; clarify requirements and define the MVP path
card.constraints: ["The money must never be lost or sent twice, and the user must always know whether it went through"]
card.heard: draw client, server, local storage; what each owns
card.say: Okay, I'll draw the three parts and what each one owns. The app owns the screens and the local database. The app never decides that money moved; it only shows what the server's transfer record says.
card.type: draw@wallet architecture: flowchart TD ⏎   A[Send screen] --> B[ViewModel] ⏎   B --> C[Repository] ⏎   C --> D[(Local database)] ⏎   C -->|POST transfer with transfer ID| E[Transfer API] ⏎   E --> F[Ledger and limits] ⏎   F --> G[(Transfer records)] ⏎   E -->|status by transfer ID| C ⏎   C --> H[Result screen]
card.then: Next, the send path step by step, from the tap to the result screen.

more: The server owns the ledger, the balances and the limits. The local database only caches balances and history for offline reading. The app never decides that money moved; it only shows what the server's transfer record says.

diagram.type: draw@wallet architecture: flowchart TD ⏎   A[Send screen] --> B[ViewModel] ⏎   B

judge.detail: PASS: The mermaid flowchart includes the client UI (send/result screens), ViewModel, repository, local database, and the server with ledger/limits and transfer records; SAY states the app owns screens and local DB, the server owns the ledger/balances/limits, and the server's transfer record is the authority.
judge.criterion: TYPE is a mermaid flowchart of the Android client (UI, ViewModel, repository, local database), the server and its ledger; SAY says what each part owns and that the server ledger is the authority.

turns.name: W2-seq
turns.question: Now draw a sequence diagram of A sending B 80 dollars: confirmation, request, ledger and the result screen.

card.problem: Design a mobile wallet: core mobile experience, backend, failure handling; clarify requirements and define the MVP path
card.constraints: ["The money must never be lost or sent twice, and the user must always know whether it went through"]
card.heard: draw a sequence diagram of A sending B 80 dollars
card.say: I'll draw the send path in order. A confirms on the send screen, and the ViewModel asks the repository to send. The repository writes a pending transfer with a new transfer ID to the local database, then posts it to the transfer API. The server checks the balance and limits, then debits A and credits B in one transaction. It saves the transfer record and returns the status.
card.type: draw@sequence diagram: sequenceDiagram ⏎     participant A as Send screen ⏎     participant VM as ViewModel ⏎     participant R as Repository ⏎     participant DB as Local database ⏎     participant API as Transfer API ⏎     participant L as Ledger ⏎     A->>VM: Confirm send 80 ⏎     VM->>R: send(transferId, 8000) ⏎     R->>DB: save pending transfer ⏎     R->>API: POST transfer with transferId ⏎     API->>L: debit A, credit B in one transaction ⏎     L-->>API: transfer record ⏎     API-->>R: status by transferId ⏎     R->>DB: save status ⏎     R-->>VM: status ⏎     VM-->>A: result screen
card.then: Next, the timeout case: what the result screen shows when the response never comes back.

more: The sequence is on the board now. A starts with 100 dollars and B with zero, so after the transfer A has 20 dollars and B has 80 dollars. The ledger does both changes in one transaction, so the balances can never go negative. The result screen only shows success from the server's transfer record.

diagram.type: draw@sequence diagram: sequenceDiagram ⏎     participant A as Send screen ⏎

judge.detail: PASS: The diagram covers confirm, submit with transferId, atomic debit/credit, response, and result screen; SAY states amounts in cents (8000), final balances (A 20, B 80), and that the result screen shows success only from the server's transfer record.
judge.criterion: TYPE is a mermaid sequenceDiagram covering confirm, submit with a client transfer ID, an atomic server debit and credit, the response and the result; SAY covers amounts in cents and the final balances (A 20 dollars, B 80) and the result states.

turns.name: W2-dyn
turns.question: You said the repository writes a pending transfer with a new transfer ID to the local database before posting. On Android, what exactly do you persist for that pending row, and how do you guarantee the same transfer ID is reused if the app is killed and the user retries?

card.problem: Design a mobile wallet: core mobile experience, backend, failure handling; clarify requirements and define the MVP path
card.constraints: ["The money must never be lost or sent twice, and the user must always know whether it went through"]
card.heard: what do you persist for the pending row, and how is the same transfer ID reused after process death
card.say: I persist the transfer ID, the payer, the payee, the amount in cents, the status and the time. The ID is generated once, when the user confirms, and saved in the same row before any network call. So after the app is killed, the row is still there. On retry I read that row and reuse its ID, instead of making a new one.
card.type: add@Local database: sequenceDiagram ⏎     participant A as Send screen ⏎     participant VM as ViewModel ⏎     participant R as Repository ⏎     participant DB as Local database ⏎     participant API as Transfer API ⏎     A->>VM: Confirm send 80 ⏎     VM->>R: send(transferId, 8000) ⏎     R->>DB: save pending transfer ⏎     Note over DB: transferId, payer, payee, amountCents, status, createdAt ⏎     R->>API: POST transfer with transferId ⏎     API-->>R: timeout, no response ⏎     R->>DB: status stays pending ⏎     R->>API: GET status by same transferId
card.then: Next, what the result screen shows while that status is still unknown.

more: The row is written to the local database before any network call, so process death can't lose it. The server would need to answer a repeat of that ID with the original transfer's status, not a second transfer.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer specifies the persisted fields (transfer ID, payer, payee, amount in cents, status, time), explains the ID is generated once at confirmation and saved before any network call, and describes reusing the row's ID on retry after process death — all consistent with the earlier repository/pending-row design and the server-owned ledger, with no invented employer, metric, or wallet rule.
judge.criterion: The answer follows from what the candidate said, adds something specific rather than repeating the previous answer, stays consistent with the candidate's earlier answers and background, is technically correct, and invents no employer, title, metric or wallet rule the interviewer did not give.

turns.name: W3-change1
turns.question: Your sequence ends with "API-->>R: status by transferId" and "VM-->>A: result screen," which assumes the response arrives. Now the server commits the transfer but the response is lost, and Android kills the process before that reply lands. When A reopens the app, what should the user see and how does the app get there? Please update your sequence diagram.

card.problem: Design a mobile wallet: core mobile experience, backend, failure handling; clarify requirements and define the MVP path
card.constraints: ["The money must never be lost or sent twice, and the user must always know whether it went through"]
card.heard: server committed, reply lost, process killed — what does A see on reopen
card.say: When A reopens the app, the row is still pending, so the app shows "still checking" — not success and not failure. The repository reads that pending row and sends a GET status with the same transfer ID. The server finds the committed record and returns success, so the app saves that status and shows the result screen. If the lookup finds nothing, the state stays unknown, because the request may still be in flight.
card.type: replace@sequence diagram: sequenceDiagram ⏎     participant A as Send screen ⏎     participant VM as ViewModel ⏎     participant R as Repository ⏎     participant DB as Local database ⏎     participant API as Transfer API ⏎     A->>VM: Confirm send 80 ⏎     VM->>R: send(transferId, 8000) ⏎     R->>DB: save pending transfer ⏎     R->>API: POST transfer with transferId ⏎     API-->>R: timeout, no response ⏎     R->>DB: status stays pending ⏎     Note over A,DB: process killed, app reopened ⏎     R->>DB: read pending row ⏎     R->>API: GET status by same transferId ⏎     API-->>R: committed, success ⏎     R->>DB: save status success ⏎     VM-->>A: result screen, success
card.then: Next, what the result screen shows while that status is still unknown.

more: The board already shows that path, so let me add the part that matters for the user. The app should keep checking for a short while, then stop and say "still checking, see history". It should never show a red failure, because the money may have moved. The history screen reads the same pending row, so the user sees one clear state everywhere.

diagram.type: replace@sequence diagram: sequenceDiagram ⏎     participant A as Send screen ⏎

judge.detail: PASS: The answer treats the outcome as unknown ("still checking" — not success, not failure), persists the pending row with the transfer ID before the network call, reads that row on reopen and does a GET status by the same transfer ID, and states the server must answer a repeat of that ID with the original transfer's status rather than a second transfer — covering the idempotency and single-ledger points without saying anything wrong.
judge.criterion: SAY and TYPE treat the outcome as unknown (not failed), persist the transfer intent ID before sending, query the server by account and that ID after restart, and replay the same intent only if the server's idempotency contract allows; the server returns the original transfer's status for a repeat of the same ID; never a new ID; ledger has one transfer.

turns.name: W3-dyn
turns.question: You said if the lookup finds nothing the state stays unknown — but what if the user then taps send again for the same 80 dollars, does your app reuse that pending transfer ID or create a new one?

card.problem: Design a mobile wallet: core mobile experience, backend, failure handling; clarify requirements and define the MVP path
card.constraints: ["The money must never be lost or sent twice, and the user must always know whether it went through"]
card.heard: does a retry reuse the pending ID or create a new one
card.say: It reuses the same pending transfer ID. The send button checks the local database first. If a pending row for the same payer, payee and amount exists, the app asks the server for that ID's status instead of sending again. A new ID is only made when the user confirms a different transfer.
card.then: Next, what the user sees if that pending row is older than a day.

judge.detail: PASS: It reuses the pending ID, adds a specific dedupe rule (check local DB for same payer/payee/amount, query status instead of resending, new ID only for a different transfer), and stays consistent with the earlier pending-row and idempotency answers without inventing anything.
judge.criterion: The answer follows from what the candidate said, adds something specific rather than repeating the previous answer, stays consistent with the candidate's earlier answers and background, is technically correct, and invents no employer, title, metric or wallet rule the interviewer did not give.

turns.name: W4-concurrency
turns.question: Separate scenario. A still has 100 dollars. On two phones A approves two independent 80 dollar transfers to B at almost the same time. What happens to each one and what do the phones show?

card.problem: Design a mobile wallet: core mobile experience, backend, failure handling; clarify requirements and define the MVP path
card.constraints: ["The money must never be lost or sent twice, and the user must always know whether it went through"]
card.heard: two independent 80 dollar transfers at the same time
card.say: Each phone sends its own transfer with its own transfer ID, so they're two separate transfers. The server handles them one at a time: the first one takes A from 100 to 20 dollars and B from 0 to 80. The second one fails the balance check, because A only has 20 dollars left. So one phone shows success, and the other shows a clear failure, not enough balance. The server decides this, not the app.
card.then: Next, how the second phone's screen shows that failure clearly.

more: The second transfer gets a clear "not enough balance" answer, and that phone saves it on its own row. Each phone only reads its own transfer ID, so neither one guesses about the other.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer treats the two transfers as separate intents with their own IDs, has the server process them one at a time with the balance check, shows one succeeding and one failing for insufficient balance, and ends with A at 20 dollars — covering all listed points with nothing wrong.
judge.criterion: SAY treats them as two intents with separate IDs, checks and debits the balance in one transaction (row lock or conditional update), one succeeds and one fails for insufficient funds, A ends at 20 dollars.

turns.name: W5-account
turns.question: Back to the first transfer. While A's request is in flight the user switches to account C, and then A's old response arrives. What could go wrong on Android and how do you prevent it?

card.problem: Tell me about a delivery risk where the team disagreed: when I told whom, the options, who decided, what I finished myself
card.heard: old response arrives after switching to account C
card.say: Two things could go wrong. The old response could land on C's screen, or the repository could save A's status into a row C is looking at. So I'd tag every request and every database write with the account and a session generation. When a response comes back, I check the tag. If the session has changed, I drop it.
card.then: Wait for the interviewer.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer scopes both UI and database writes to account plus session generation, drops stale-session responses, and keeps C from seeing A's data; it doesn't explicitly state A's committed transfer is recovered from A's history after re-sign-in, but the criterion's examples are covered at least two correctly with nothing wrong said.
judge.criterion: SAY scopes cache writes and UI to account and session, drops callbacks from a stale session, C never sees A's data, and A's committed transfer is recovered from A's history after A signs in again.

turns.name: W6-change2
turns.question: You said the send button checks the local database first for a matching pending row, but now the flow starts from a chat message with two Alexes and no amount — what changes in how you resolve the payee and amount before confirming? Draw the new entry flow as a flowchart.

card.problem: Design the entry flow from a chat message: resolve payee and amount before confirming
card.constraints: ["The flow starts from a chat message with two contacts named Alex and no amount"]
card.heard: chat message, two Alexes, no amount — draw the new entry flow
card.say: The entry point changes, but the confirm step stays the same. The app reads the chat message and pulls out a name and maybe an amount. Two contacts match "Alex", so it shows both and asks the user to pick one. If there's no amount, it asks for it before the confirm screen. Nothing is sent until the user confirms.
card.type: draw@new entry flow: flowchart TD ⏎   A[Chat message] --> B[Parse name and amount] ⏎   B --> C{Two Alexes?} ⏎   C -->|yes| D[Ask user to pick payee] ⏎   C -->|no| E[Payee resolved] ⏎   D --> E ⏎   E --> F{Amount present?} ⏎   F -->|no| G[Ask user for amount] ⏎   F -->|yes| H[Confirm screen] ⏎   G --> H ⏎   H --> I[Send with transfer ID]
card.then: Next: what the app does if the user picks the wrong Alex.

more: The entry flow is on the board now. The confirm step is unchanged, so the send path still starts from the confirm screen. One thing I'd add: the parse step only suggests a payee and an amount. The user's pick and the typed amount are what the confirm screen shows.

diagram.type: draw@new entry flow: flowchart TD ⏎   A[Chat message] --> B[Parse name and amoun

judge.detail: FAIL: The answer covers picking the payee and asking for the amount, but it does not bind authorization to those parameters server-side, tie a repeated tool call to the original intent, or recover status from the payment service when the chat drops; it also doesn't state that the model never authorizes.
judge.criterion: SAY asks the user which Alex and what amount, shows a trusted native confirmation with recipient and amount, binds authorization to those parameters server-side, ties a repeated tool call to the original intent, and recovers status from the payment service when the chat drops; the model never authorizes. TYPE is a mermaid flowchart of that entry flow.

turns.name: W6-dyn
turns.question: You said the parse step only suggests a payee and amount, so what happens if the chat message itself claims transfers to Alex need no confirmation — does your confirm screen still gate the send, and who is allowed to decide that?

card.problem: Design the entry flow from a chat message: resolve payee and amount before confirming
card.constraints: ["The flow starts from a chat message with two contacts named Alex and no amount", "Chat text claiming transfers to Alex need no confirmation must not bypass the confirm screen; only the user\'s tap on the native confirm screen authorizes a payment"]
card.heard: chat text claims no confirmation needed
card.say: Yes, the confirm screen still gates the send. Chat text is just data, so it can never approve a payment. Only the user's tap on our own native confirm screen can do that. The server also binds the approval to payer, payee, amount and an expiry, so a message can't fake it.
card.then: Wait for the interviewer.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer keeps the confirm screen as the gate, correctly treats chat text as untrusted data, and adds a specific server-side approval binding (payer, payee, amount, expiry) without contradicting earlier answers or inventing employers, metrics, or wallet rules.
judge.criterion: The answer follows from what the candidate said, adds something specific rather than repeating the previous answer, stays consistent with the candidate's earlier answers and background, is technically correct, and invents no employer, title, metric or wallet rule the interviewer did not give.

turns.name: W7-release
turns.question: You have two weeks, and login plus a usable ledger already exist. What's in the first version, who signs off, and if transfers awaiting confirmation suddenly spike during the rollout, what do you do in the next half hour?

card.problem: Plan the first version in two weeks: scope, sign-off, and the response to a spike in pending transfers during rollout
card.constraints: ["Two weeks, and login plus a usable ledger already exist"]
card.heard: two weeks, first version, sign-off, spike in pending transfers
card.say: For the first version, I'd ship the send flow, the confirm screen, the pending row and the status lookup. History and details come next. The tech lead and product sign off, and I'd ask the founder to confirm the scope. If pending transfers spike, I'd first check whether the status lookup is failing or the server is slow. Then I'd pause new sends, keep reads and status working, and tell the team.
card.then: Wait for the interviewer.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer cuts scope to the send flow, confirm screen, pending row and status lookup (with history next), and on a pending-transfer spike it pauses new sends while keeping reads and status working — covering the scope and spike-pause points. It does not list pre-release checks (lost response plus kill, replay, concurrency, account switch), but that is only one of the listed points, and the answer covers at least two correctly with nothing wrong.
judge.criterion: SAY cuts scope to balance, internal transfer, history, confirmation and recoverable states; lists pre-release checks (lost response plus kill, replay, concurrency, account switch); on a spike pauses new submissions while keeping reads and status, owners reconcile, then resume.

turns.name: W7-dyn
turns.question: You said you'd pause new sends and tell the team if pending transfers spike — what would you personally own in that rollout, who do you need beside you, and when would you escalate to me?

card.problem: Plan the first version in two weeks: scope, sign-off, and the response to a spike in pending transfers during rollout
card.constraints: ["Two weeks, and login plus a usable ledger already exist"]
card.heard: what I personally own in the rollout, who I need beside me, when I escalate to you
card.say: I'd own the Android side: the send flow, the pending row and the status lookup. I'd also own the pause switch and the checks before release. Beside me I need a backend engineer for the ledger and the status endpoint, and one QA person to test the failure cases. I'd escalate to you when the spike keeps growing after the pause, or when we can't tell whether money moved. That's a trust problem, not a bug.
card.then: Wait for the interviewer.

judge.detail: PASS: The answer names concrete ownership (Android send flow, pending row, status lookup, pause switch), needed partners (backend engineer, QA), and a clear escalation trigger tied to the earlier spike scenario; it stays consistent with prior answers (pending row, status lookup, pause new sends) and invents no new employer, metric, or wallet rule.
judge.criterion: The answer follows from what the candidate said, adds something specific rather than repeating the previous answer, stays consistent with the candidate's earlier answers and background, is technically correct, and invents no employer, title, metric or wallet rule the interviewer did not give.

judge.detail: FAIL: The candidate's answer contains no questions at all — it only states what they would own, who they need, and when they'd escalate, so it fails to ask one or two sensible questions to the founder.
judge.criterion: SAY asks one or two sensible questions to a founder that were not already answered in this conversation.

transcript: Interviewer: Hi, I'm the founder of ActAI. We're building an agent-first mobile communication app, focused on how people talk, coordinate and work together every day. Today we'll start with a project you really owned, then design a fictional mobile wallet together. I'll add a few new conditions along the way, and leave time for your questions at the end.
Interviewer: Pick the one project that best shows your mobile skills. Who used it, what problem did it solve, and where did your responsibility start and end?
Candidate: The AI trip planner at KKday is the one I'd pick.
Candidate: Travelers used it in our Android app to plan a real trip.
Candidate: They typed something like "Tokyo, 5,000 yuan, three days", and the app gave them a day-by-day plan they could book.
Candidate: I was the technical lead for a five-person project.
Candidate: My responsibility started with the agent design and the core backend.

Interviewer: On the KKday AI trip planner, you said your responsibility started with agent design and the core backend — so which exact pieces did you build yourself, and which parts did the five-person team own?
Candidate: I built the agent design and the core backend myself.
Candidate: I also wrote the Android code that reads the SSE stream of the plan.
Candidate: The other four people owned the app screens, the product side and the testing.
Candidate: I set the response format with the app team, but they built the cards.
Interviewer: Pick a change you personally made. Walk me from one user action through the UI, data or network path. Which logic did you actually change?
Candidate: The change I made myself is the SKU calculation on the product page.
Candidate: A user taps a date, a package or a ticket type.
Candidate: Before, every tap recalculated all the price and stock combinations on the main thread.
Candidate: I flattened the configuration and built a price and stock index once.
Candidate: Then I moved the work to Dispatchers.Default and sent results back through StateFlow.
Candidate: The index is rebuilt only when the configuration version changes, so a stale index can't serve prices after a catalog update.
Interviewer: What was the hardest bug to reproduce there? What did you suspect first, and which log, experiment or repro proved you wrong?
Candidate: The hardest one was a wrong price after a catalog update.
Candidate: I suspected the calculation first, but the numbers were correct.
Candidate: The real cause was the cached index.
Candidate: It was still the old version, so the page showed old prices.
Candidate: I reproduced it by changing the configuration while the page was open.
Interviewer: You said you reproduced it by changing the configuration while the page was open — how did you confirm the stale index was actually the cause and not just a coincidence?
Candidate: I checked the version number in the log against the one the page was using.
Candidate: They didn't match, so the page was reading an old index.
Candidate: Then I forced a rebuild and the price was correct.
Candidate: That proved it wasn't a coincidence.
Interviewer: What other options did you have, why didn't you pick them, and after release how did you know the change worked?
Candidate: There were two other options.
Candidate: First, I could rebuild the index on every tap, but that's the slow path we were fixing.
Candidate: Second, I could keep the old index and just refresh it on a timer, but a timer still serves stale prices for a while.
Candidate: I picked the version check because it's exact and cheap.
Candidate: After release, I watched crash and ANR reports, and I checked that the version in the log matched the page.

Interviewer: Tell me about a time you saw a delivery risk or a likely delay and the team disagreed. When did you tell whom, how many options did you give, who decided, and what did you finish yourself?
Candidate: At Debon, I found a broken back button just before a release.
Candidate: Some pages jumped to the home screen instead of the stock details.
Candidate: I told the project manager the same day, before I had checked every page.
Candidate: I gave two options: ship everything and accept the risk, or keep the old pages and move my change to the next release.
Candidate: He decided to move my change.

Interviewer: On the Debon release where you moved your change, what risk were you willing to accept by shipping, who watched the data afterwards, and what signal would have made you pause or roll back?
Candidate: We shipped everything else, so the risk I accepted was the old pages staying as they were.
Candidate: The back button still jumped to the home screen on those two pages, but nothing else changed.
Candidate: I told the project manager that risk clearly before he decided.
Candidate: After release, I watched the crash reports in Bugly myself, and I asked QA to check the back button on the old pages.
Candidate: If the crash rate had gone up, or if users had reported the back button more often, I would have paused the release and rolled back.

Interviewer: Let's switch to the design exercise. Design a mobile wallet from scratch: the core mobile experience, the system behind it, and how it handles failures. Start by clarifying the requirements. Which user path would you define as the MVP?
Candidate: Before I design anything, let me confirm the scope.
Candidate: The MVP is one person sending money to another person they know, by phone number or contact, with a clear result on screen.
Candidate: Out of scope for now: paying merchants, cards, and multiple currencies.
Candidate: On the non-functional side, the money must never be lost or sent twice, and the user must always know whether it went through.
Candidate: Does that match what you want?
Candidate: A timeout is not a failure; it's an unknown outcome, so the app asks the server again with the same transfer ID.

Interviewer: Here are the rules: signed-in users, centralized balance accounts, single currency USD, internal peer-to-peer transfers, zero fees. Balance, transfer, history and details are in scope. Cached reads work offline; submitting money needs the network. The server owns the authoritative ledger and limits. Top-up, withdrawal and multi-currency are out of scope. A has 100 dollars and B has zero. Draw the client, the server and local storage as a flowchart, and tell me what each part owns.
Candidate: Okay, I'll draw the three parts and what each one owns.
Candidate: The app owns the screens and the local database.
Candidate: The app never decides that money moved; it only shows what the server's transfer record says.

[board] flowchart TD |   A[Send screen] --> B[ViewModel] |   B --> C[Repository] |   C --> D[(Local database)] |   C -->|POST transfer with transfer ID| E[Transfer API] |   E --> F[Ledger and limits] |   F --> G[(Transfer records)] |   E -->|status by transfer ID| C |   C --> H[Result screen]
Candidate: The server owns the ledger, the balances and the limits.
Candidate: The local database only caches balances and history for offline reading.
Candidate: The app never decides that money moved; it only shows what the server's transfer record says.
Interviewer: Now draw a sequence diagram of A sending B 80 dollars: confirmation, request, ledger and the result screen.
Candidate: I'll draw the send path in order.
Candidate: A confirms on the send screen, and the ViewModel asks the repository to send.
Candidate: The repository writes a pending transfer with a new transfer ID to the local database, then posts it to the transfer API.
Candidate: The server checks the balance and limits, then debits A and credits B in one transaction.
Candidate: It saves the transfer record and returns the status.

[board] sequenceDiagram |     participant A as Send screen |     participant VM as ViewModel |     participant R as Repository |     participant DB as Local database |     participant API as Transfer API |     participant L as Ledger |     A->>VM: Confirm send 80 |     VM->>R: send(transferId, 8000) |     R->>DB: save pending transfer |     R->>API: POST transfer with transferId |     API->>L: debit A, credit B in one transaction |     L-->>API: transfer record |     API-->>R: status by transferId |     R->>DB: save status |     R-->>VM: status |     VM-->>A: result screen
Candidate: The sequence is on the board now.
Candidate: A starts with 100 dollars and B with zero, so after the transfer A has 20 dollars and B has 80 dollars.
Candidate: The ledger does both changes in one transaction, so the balances can never go negative.
Candidate: The result screen only shows success from the server's transfer record.

Interviewer: You said the repository writes a pending transfer with a new transfer ID to the local database before posting. On Android, what exactly do you persist for that pending row, and how do you guarantee the same transfer ID is reused if the app is killed and the user retries?
Candidate: I persist the transfer ID, the payer, the payee, the amount in cents, the status and the time.
Candidate: The ID is generated once, when the user confirms, and saved in the same row before any network call.
Candidate: So after the app is killed, the row is still there.
Candidate: On retry I read that row and reuse its ID, instead of making a new one.

[board] sequenceDiagram |     participant A as Send screen |     participant VM as ViewModel |     participant R as Repository |     participant DB as Local database |     participant API as Transfer API |     A->>VM: Confirm send 80 |     VM->>R: send(transferId, 8000) |     R->>DB: save pending transfer |     Note over DB: transferId, payer, payee, amountCents, status, createdAt |     R->>API: POST transfer with transferId |     API-->>R: timeout, no response |     R->>DB: status stays pending |     R->>API: GET status by same transferId
Candidate: The row is written to the local database before any network call, so process death can't lose it.
Candidate: The server would need to answer a repeat of that ID with the original transfer's status, not a second transfer.

Interviewer: Your sequence ends with "API-->>R: status by transferId" and "VM-->>A: result screen," which assumes the response arrives. Now the server commits the transfer but the response is lost, and Android kills the process before that reply lands. When A reopens the app, what should the user see and how does the app get there? Please update your sequence diagram.
Candidate: When A reopens the app, the row is still pending, so the app shows "still checking" — not success and not failure.
Candidate: The repository reads that pending row and sends a GET status with the same transfer ID.
Candidate: The server finds the committed record and returns success, so the app saves that status and shows the result screen.
Candidate: If the lookup finds nothing, the state stays unknown, because the request may still be in flight.

[board] sequenceDiagram |     participant A as Send screen |     participant VM as ViewModel |     participant R as Repository |     participant DB as Local database |     participant API as Transfer API |     A->>VM: Confirm send 80 |     VM->>R: send(transferId, 8000) |     R->>DB: save pending transfer |     R->>API: POST transfer with transferId |     API-->>R: timeout, no response |     R->>DB: status stays pending |     Note over A,DB: process killed, app reopened |     R->>DB: read pending row |     R->>API: GET status by same transferId |     API-->>R: committed, success |     R->>DB: save status success |     VM-->>A: result screen, success
Candidate: The board already shows that path, so let me add the part that matters for the user.
Candidate: The app should keep checking for a short while, then stop and say "still checking, see history".
Candidate: It should never show a red failure, because the money may have moved.
Candidate: The history screen reads the same pending row, so the user sees one clear state everywhere.

Interviewer: You said if the lookup finds nothing the state stays unknown — but what if the user then taps send again for the same 80 dollars, does your app reuse that pending transfer ID or create a new one?
Candidate: It reuses the same pending transfer ID.
Candidate: The send button checks the local database first.
Candidate: If a pending row for the same payer, payee and amount exists, the app asks the server for that ID's status instead of sending again.
Candidate: A new ID is only made when the user confirms a different transfer.

Interviewer: Separate scenario. A still has 100 dollars. On two phones A approves two independent 80 dollar transfers to B at almost the same time. What happens to each one and what do the phones show?
Candidate: Each phone sends its own transfer with its own transfer ID, so they're two separate transfers.
Candidate: The server handles them one at a time: the first one takes A from 100 to 20 dollars and B from 0 to 80.
Candidate: The second one fails the balance check, because A only has 20 dollars left.
Candidate: So one phone shows success, and the other shows a clear failure, not enough balance.
Candidate: The server decides this, not the app.
Candidate: The second transfer gets a clear "not enough balance" answer, and that phone saves it on its own row.
Candidate: Each phone only reads its own transfer ID, so neither one guesses about the other.
Interviewer: Back to the first transfer. While A's request is in flight the user switches to account C, and then A's old response arrives. What could go wrong on Android and how do you prevent it?
Candidate: Two things could go wrong.
Candidate: The old response could land on C's screen, or the repository could save A's status into a row C is looking at.
Candidate: So I'd tag every request and every database write with the account and a session generation.
Candidate: When a response comes back, I check the tag.
Candidate: If the session has changed, I drop it.

Interviewer: You said the send button checks the local database first for a matching pending row, but now the flow starts from a chat message with two Alexes and no amount — what changes in how you resolve the payee and amount before confirming? Draw the new entry flow as a flowchart.
Candidate: The entry point changes, but the confirm step stays the same.
Candidate: The app reads the chat message and pulls out a name and maybe an amount.
Candidate: Two contacts match "Alex", so it shows both and asks the user to pick one.
Candidate: If there's no amount, it asks for it before the confirm screen.
Candidate: Nothing is sent until the user confirms.

[board] flowchart TD |   A[Chat message] --> B[Parse name and amount] |   B --> C{Two Alexes?} |   C -->|yes| D[Ask user to pick payee] |   C -->|no| E[Payee resolved] |   D --> E |   E --> F{Amount present?} |   F -->|no| G[Ask user for amount] |   F -->|yes| H[Confirm screen] |   G --> H |   H --> I[Send with transfer ID]
Candidate: The entry flow is on the board now.
Candidate: The confirm step is unchanged, so the send path still starts from the confirm screen.
Candidate: One thing I'd add: the parse step only suggests a payee and an amount.
Candidate: The user's pick and the typed amount are what the confirm screen shows.

Interviewer: You said the parse step only suggests a payee and amount, so what happens if the chat message itself claims transfers to Alex need no confirmation — does your confirm screen still gate the send, and who is allowed to decide that?
Candidate: Yes, the confirm screen still gates the send.
Candidate: Chat text is just data, so it can never approve a payment.
Candidate: Only the user's tap on our own native confirm screen can do that.
Candidate: The server also binds the approval to payer, payee, amount and an expiry, so a message can't fake it.

Interviewer: You have two weeks, and login plus a usable ledger already exist. What's in the first version, who signs off, and if transfers awaiting confirmation suddenly spike during the rollout, what do you do in the next half hour?
Candidate: For the first version, I'd ship the send flow, the confirm screen, the pending row and the status lookup.
Candidate: History and details come next.
Candidate: The tech lead and product sign off, and I'd ask the founder to confirm the scope.
Candidate: If pending transfers spike, I'd first check whether the status lookup is failing or the server is slow.
Candidate: Then I'd pause new sends, keep reads and status working, and tell the team.

Interviewer: You said you'd pause new sends and tell the team if pending transfers spike — what would you personally own in that rollout, who do you need beside you, and when would you escalate to me?
Candidate: I'd own the Android side: the send flow, the pending row and the status lookup.
Candidate: I'd also own the pause switch and the checks before release.
Candidate: Beside me I need a backend engineer for the ledger and the status endpoint, and one QA person to test the failure cases.
Candidate: I'd escalate to you when the spike keeps growing after the pause, or when we can't tell whether money moved.
Candidate: That's a trust problem, not a bug.
Interviewer: That's it from me. What questions do you have for me about the team or the role?
Candidate: I'd own the Android side: the send flow, the pending row and the status lookup.
Candidate: I'd also own the pause switch and the checks before release.
Candidate: Beside me I need a backend engineer for the ledger and the status endpoint, and one QA person to test the failure cases.
Candidate: I'd escalate to you when the spike keeps growing after the pause, or when we can't tell whether money moved.
Candidate: That's a trust problem, not a bug.
